Hook: Every month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics records about a hundred thousand prices, from about twenty-three thousand shops and service businesses across America, to build the consumer price index. In 2004, Mark Bils and Peter Klenow opened those records and did something simple: they counted how often each price changes. The median price lasted about four months, far less time than economists had been assuming. And yet, as this part will show, long enough for money to move the real economy.

Here is what that difference does. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta splits the consumer price index, food and energy aside, into two groups by how often each item's price changes. In orange, the prices that change often: clothing, cars, hotel rooms. In blue, the prices that change rarely: rents, haircuts, insurance and fees. In 2022 the flexible prices rose 19 percent in a year, the sticky ones 6.5. The flexible line jumps with every shock; the sticky one moves slowly and carries the trend. If all prices behaved like the orange line, money would barely matter for output. Because so many behave like the blue one, it does.

This part's question: why does money move the real economy, and what is the best a central bank can do? How sticky are prices, and why? What do sticky prices do to the whole economy? The answer fits in three equations, which now sit inside every central bank. And what should a central bank do with them, including when interest rates cannot fall any further?
Economics, Built. Part thirty: sticky prices.

Here is the plan. A guess about how long prices last, then the evidence, and why prices stick at all. Calvo's model of price setting, and the Phillips curve it implies, derived. The household's side as a dynamic IS curve, the central bank as a Taylor rule, and the three equations solved together. When stabilizing inflation also stabilizes output, what the best policy looks like, and why menu costs can make money matter less than Calvo says. And the zero lower bound, the puzzle of forward guidance, the bigger models central banks actually use, and a dial.
Evidence: Chapter two. The evidence on price setting.

There are three ways to find out how prices are set. Follow one product for decades. Stephen Cecchetti followed the newsstand prices of American magazines, and found they changed rarely, and more often when inflation was high. Ask. Alan Blinder and his coauthors interviewed the price setters of two hundred American firms in the 1990s: the median firm changed its price about once a year. The explanation they rated highest was coordination: nobody wants to raise prices first. Contracts with customers, written or understood, also ranked high. Or read the records, as Bils, Klenow, Nakamura and Steinsson did. All three agree. Many prices stay fixed for months, even though some change every week.

The Atlanta Fed's two indexes show what the difference does in calmer times. From 1985 to 2019, inflation in the flexible prices had a standard deviation of 1.6 points; in the sticky prices, 1.1. A price that will be in force for months has to be set with the future in mind. So sticky-price inflation carries what firms expect, and Michael Bryan and Brent Meyer found it the better guide to where inflation is heading.

That is one of the series' facts. In the data, the median price lasts four point three months counting sales, eight to eleven without. The theory of why comes next. And the Island's prices, from chapter five on, last nine months on average, the calibration in Jordi Galí's textbook, between the two.
Menu: Chapter three. Why prices stick: menu costs.

Back on the Island, Bo's ferry fare is painted on a board by the pier. Repainting it is a nuisance, and regular passengers dislike surprises. Bo faces a demand elasticity of 6, so his best fare is 20 percent above his cost. Now suppose demand falls, and his best fare falls with it, but the old fare stays on the board. In gold, Bo's profit, against how far his fare is from the best one. In green, the number of passengers he carries. With a fare five percent too high, his profit is only 3.1 percent below the best he could do, but he carries 26 percent fewer passengers. The top of a profit curve is flat: near the best price, a mistake costs the seller very little.

Here are the numbers. A fare one percent too high costs Bo 0.14 percent of his profit, and the island 5.8 percent of its ferry trips: forty times as much. At two percent, twenty times. At five percent, eight times. At ten percent, four times. The reason is general. The loss of profit grows with the square of the gap, because the profit curve is flat at the top; the loss of output grows with the gap itself.

In 1985 Gregory Mankiw turned this into an argument about the whole economy. For a firm, leaving its price alone after a small change in demand costs almost nothing: a loss of the second order. But the output lost to society is of the first order. So even a tiny cost of changing prices, a menu cost, can be enough to keep prices where they are, and then a fall in the money supply cuts output instead of prices. George Akerlof and Janet Yellen made the same point the same year: firms that are only nearly rational lose little, while the economy loses a lot. It is the reason money is not neutral, in one picture.
Markup: Chapter four. Monopolistic competition: the desired markup.

Sticky prices need firms that set prices, so the model starts from Part twelve's monopolistic competition. Each firm sells its own variety, and its sales fall with its price relative to the average, with elasticity epsilon. Each firm sets its own price, and the best price is a fixed markup on marginal cost. With epsilon at 6, twenty percent. That markup does a quiet but essential job. Because price is above marginal cost, a firm is always glad to sell one more unit at its going price, so when demand rises and its price is stuck, it simply produces more.

Here is that firm when demand rises. Demand moves out, from grey to green. The price is stuck at its old level. Marginal cost rises as the firm produces more, because it must pay more for overtime and materials. The firm sells more at the old price, and its markup shrinks, but it remains positive. So output is set by demand, not by the price: exactly Keynes's effective demand, now derived from firms that choose. And the gap between what the firm would like to charge and what it does charge drives the next chapter.
Calvo: Chapter five. Calvo's fairy: the New Keynesian Phillips curve.

How should sticky prices enter a model of the whole economy? Guillermo Calvo's answer, in 1983, is a fairy. Each quarter, a randomly chosen fraction of firms, one minus theta, may reset their price; the rest must keep the price they have. With theta at two thirds, a third of firms reset each quarter, whatever has happened to them and however long they have waited. A price then lasts 9 months on average. As a description of a firm, it is absurd: no firm waits for a fairy. As mathematics it is wonderful, because the firms that reset are a random sample, so one equation describes them all.

Now take a firm the fairy has visited. It knows its new price may last a long time, so it looks ahead. In logs, its best price is its markup plus a weighted average of the nominal marginal costs it expects in every future quarter, each weighted by the chance that the price will still be in force then, theta to the power k, and by discounting. And the price level is an average of the new prices and the old ones: a third reset, two thirds carried over from last quarter.

Put the two equations together, use the fact that marginal cost rises with the output gap, the percentage gap between output and what it would be with flexible prices, and out comes the New Keynesian Phillips curve: inflation today equals beta times expected inflation next quarter, plus kappa times the output gap. Kappa, the slope, shrinks as prices get stickier, as theta rises, and depends on how fast costs rise with output. Now solve it forward, and inflation today is kappa times the discounted sum of every output gap people expect. Compare Part twenty-eight's curve, which looked backward at last year's inflation. This one looks forward: firms raise prices today because they expect costs to be high later.

How steep is the curve? Here is kappa against theta, holding the rest of the Island's economy fixed. Stickier prices mean a flatter curve. If prices last about four months, as Bils and Klenow found, theta is about 0.5 and kappa about 0.38. Galí's baseline, prices lasting nine months, gives 0.13, which the Island uses. Nakamura and Steinsson's regular prices give about 0.09. The difference between those two numbers decides how much output a central bank must sacrifice to move inflation, the sacrifice ratio of Part twenty-eight.
Taylor: Chapter seven. A rule for the central bank.

In 1993 John Taylor proposed a rule simple enough to fit on an index card. The federal funds rate equals two, plus inflation, plus half the gap between inflation and two percent, plus half the output gap. Two is the neutral real rate; inflation is over the past year; the gap is output against its potential. So each extra point of inflation raises the policy rate by a point and a half, which means the real rate rises too: the central bank leans against inflation. And each point of output gap adds half a point.

How well does it fit? In pink, the federal funds rate from 1985 to 2007. In green, Taylor's rule, computed from the GDP deflator and the Budget Office's output gap as they stand today. Through Alan Greenspan's years as chair, the two move together, with a correlation of 0.69 and a typical gap of 1.6 points. A regression over those years puts 1.34 on inflation and 0.94 on the output gap. The number that matters is the first one: more than one for one. The next chapter shows why.

And since then? From 2009 to 2015 the rule called for a negative interest rate, as low as minus 1.3 percent, but the federal funds rate stopped just above zero. That is the zero lower bound, chapter twelve's subject. In 2021 and 2022 the rule called for much higher rates, much sooner, than the Federal Reserve set. A rule describes a central bank; it does not bind one. But as a description, it is what the model needs.
Solved: Before solving the model, check that it has one solution. Both variables, inflation and the gap, are free to jump, so by the counting rule of Part twenty-nine, both roots of the system must lie outside the unit circle. Here is the answer for every rule, the response to inflation across the bottom and to the gap up the side. In green, rules that pin down a unique equilibrium. In red, rules that leave many: any inflation people expect can come true. The boundary has a formula: kappa times phi pi minus one, plus one minus beta times phi x, must be positive. In words, the Taylor principle: when inflation rises, raise the nominal rate by more, so that the real rate rises. Taylor's own rule is safely inside. Richard Clarida, Jordi Galí and Mark Gertler estimated the Federal Reserve's response before 1979 and found it below one, and after 1979 above: one account of why the 1970s went wrong and the 1980s right.

Now the responses, with Galí's numbers on the Island: each shock is one point at an annual rate, fading by half each quarter. A monetary tightening: the policy rate rises 0.43 points, the output gap falls 0.28 percent, and inflation falls 0.29 points. Money is not neutral, because prices cannot all adjust at once. A rise in demand: output and inflation both rise, and the rule raises the rate to lean against them. A cost-push shock: inflation rises by 1.4 points while output falls 0.56 percent, because the central bank raises rates against the inflation. Demand shocks move output and inflation together; cost shocks move them apart, and that difference is the next chapter.
Coincidence: Chapter nine. The natural rate and the divine coincidence.

The IS curve's benchmark has an old name. In 1898 the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell called it the natural rate of interest: the real rate at which output equals what it would be with flexible prices. Demand shocks move it: optimism raises it, fear lowers it. So the central bank's job, in this model, is to move its rate with the natural rate. Hold the real rate below the natural rate and demand runs ahead of supply; above it, demand falls short. The trouble is that nobody can see the natural rate. It can only be estimated, as Part thirty-one does.

Now a remarkable property of the model. Suppose the central bank holds inflation at exactly its target, whatever it takes. After a demand shock, the output gap stays at zero too: moving the policy rate with the natural rate kills both at once. Olivier Blanchard and Jordi Galí called this the divine coincidence. But after a cost-push shock, holding inflation at target means an output gap of minus 1.96 percent. The coincidence holds only when nothing pushes costs up on its own: no oil shocks, no wage push, no supply chains breaking. When those happen, the central bank must choose, and the next chapter asks how.
Optimal: Chapter ten. Optimal policy: discretion and commitment.

To ask what the best policy is, first ask why inflation is costly in this model. With Calvo pricing, inflation means some prices were set recently and some long ago, so relative prices spread out. Goods that cost the same to make sell at different prices, and people buy the wrong mix of them. Michael Woodford derived the welfare loss from the household's own utility: a sum of squared inflation and squared output gaps, with a weight of kappa over epsilon on the gap. On the Island that weight is 0.021: a point of inflation costs as much as several points of output gap, because of all the price dispersion it causes.

Now a cost-push shock of one point, fading by half each quarter, and two ways to respond. Under discretion, the central bank does what is best each quarter, taking expectations as given. It splits the pain: inflation rises 0.79 points and output falls, both fading with the shock. Under commitment, it promises to keep output a little low even after the shock has gone. Because Calvo's firms look ahead, that promise lowers inflation immediately: 0.54 on impact instead of 0.79, then slightly below zero for a while. The loss falls from 0.091 to 0.057, about a third less. The promise does the work, but it is only worth anything if it is believed, and it is tempting to break later: Part twenty-eight's time inconsistency again.

The clearest difference is in the price level. Under discretion, the price level ends 0.39 percent higher and stays there: bygones are bygones. Under commitment, the brief deflation after the shock brings the price level back to where it started. So the best policy looks like targeting the price level, making up for past inflation, and that is what makes people expect lower inflation today. The Federal Reserve's move in 2020 to average inflation targeting, making up for past shortfalls, borrowed this idea, as Part thirty-one explains.
Selection: Chapter eleven. Menu costs and the selection effect.

Calvo's fairy has a hidden cost. It picks firms at random. With a real menu cost, a firm reprices when its price has drifted far enough from where it should be. After a rise in the money supply, the firms that reprice are the ones furthest below their best price, so the price changes that happen are large ones, and they do most of the adjusting. Mikhail Golosov and Robert Lucas called this the selection effect, in 2007. It can make money far less powerful than Calvo's model says, even with the same number of price changes.

Here is a race between the two, on the Island, with 20,000 firms whose best prices drift randomly from month to month. In both economies a tenth of firms reprice in a normal month. Then money rises by 5 percent. Under Calvo, prices follow slowly: half of the rise has passed into prices after 7 months. Under menu costs, the firms that were already close to repricing jump at once, and half has passed through within the first month. Measured as output, or real money, lost along the way, Calvo gives 42 percent-months, menu costs 6. The frequency of price changes is not enough to know how much money matters; which prices change matters too. Later work, with sales and multi-product firms, restores much of the effect, and the size of the selection effect is still argued.
ZLB: Chapter twelve. The zero lower bound and forward guidance.

Suppose fear grips the Island and the natural rate of interest falls to minus two percent for six quarters. The central bank should cut its rate below zero, but it cannot: people would hold cash instead. Its rate sits at zero. Output falls 5.7 percent below its natural level, and prices fall at 7.9 percent a year. Falling prices make the real interest rate higher, which deepens the slump: the liquidity trap of Part twenty-seven, now with expectations. Gauti Eggertsson and Michael Woodford worked out this case in 2003, and the numbers in the model are far larger than anything seen in 2009, which is itself a puzzle.

What can a central bank do at zero? It can talk. Promise to keep the rate at zero for a while after the natural rate has recovered, when the economy would otherwise call for higher rates. That future stimulus raises expected output and inflation, and pulls the economy up today. In the model the effect is enormous. With no promise, output is 5.7 percent below normal. Promise one extra quarter at zero, and the slump almost disappears: minus 0.7 percent. Two quarters, and it becomes a boom of 6.3 percent; three, 16 percent. No central bank has ever seen a promise work like that.

Too good to be true? Ask the model a cleaner question: promise to cut the rate by one point for one quarter, h quarters from now. A cut one quarter ahead raises today's output by 0.28 percent. A cut promised three years ahead raises it by 10 percent, with inflation up 17 points: the further away the promise, the bigger its effect today, because every quarter in between passes the stimulus back. Marco Del Negro, Marc Giannoni and Christina Patterson called this the forward guidance puzzle. Real promises are not that powerful. The repairs give households reasons not to look so far ahead: borrowing limits and income risk, as Alisdair McKay, Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson showed, or limited attention to distant news, as Xavier Gabaix proposed.
Medium: Chapter thirteen. Medium-scale models: what each friction buys.

The three-equation model has a problem with timing. After a monetary tightening, its output falls most in the very first quarter, then recovers. In the data, as Part thirty-one will measure, output's response builds for a year or more before it turns: a hump. Add three frictions to the Island: households whose consumption habits make them slow to change spending, firms that index unchanged prices to past inflation, and a central bank that moves its rate gradually. The response now builds, with the trough 2 quarters after the shock. Each friction is there to buy a feature of the data.

This is how the models central banks use were built. Lawrence Christiano, Martin Eichenbaum and Charles Evans in 2005, and Frank Smets and Raf Wouters in 2007, each added frictions to buy features of the data. Habits give the hump in spending. Sticky wages, with Calvo's fairy visiting workers too, keep inflation persistent. Indexation makes prices carry past inflation forward. Costs of adjusting investment give the hump in investment. Variable utilization lets output rise before capital does. And Smets and Wouters let seven shocks drive the economy, and estimated the whole model on American data. The critics ask whether each friction describes how people behave, or only repairs a fit.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: policy simulations at central banks.

One of the series' facts gets its theory here. In the data, as Part thirty-one will measure, output's response to a monetary tightening is hump-shaped and peaks after a year or more. The theory: habits, indexation and gradual policy spread the effect out over time. On the Island, adding them moves the trough from the moment of the shock to 2 quarters later: in the right direction, though still sooner than in the data.

Inside a central bank, the staff use these models in a few standard ways. Scenarios: what happens if oil prices jump, or if the natural rate is lower than we think? Alternative paths for the policy rate: faster, slower, following a rule, or chosen to minimize the loss. And story-telling: which shocks explain this year's forecast errors? Always alongside judgement and simpler forecasting models, never instead of them. The model's real job is to make the story add up, and to make every assumption visible.

And a forecast about the zero bound. Called it? In November 2002, Ben Bernanke, then a governor of the Federal Reserve, said that the central bank, with the rest of the government, had enough instruments to make sure that any deflation in America would be mild and brief. Six years later the federal funds rate hit zero and stayed there for seven years. Consumer prices fell over twelve months in 2009 and briefly in 2015, by at most two percent, while core inflation never went below zero. But core inflation also stayed below the two percent target most of the following decade. Right, about deflation.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: the model after 2021.

The surge of 2021 to 2023 tested this model hard. Here is what it had to learn. Flexible prices moved first, up 19 percent by February 2022, and sticky prices followed, peaking at 6.5 percent that December. When many firms reprice at once, as they did, a fairy who visits a fixed share each quarter is wrong; pricing that depends on the state of the economy fits better. The Phillips curve may steepen when labour markets are very tight, Benigno and Eggertsson's bent curve from Part twenty-eight. Supply shocks travelled through networks of firms, not as one cost-push term. And long-run expectations stayed anchored, mostly, which helped inflation fall without a recession.

The open questions follow. Is the frequency of price changes a constant, or a choice that rises when inflation does? How much does monetary policy work through people's incomes rather than through interest rates, as models with many households suggest? What does forward guidance really do, once the puzzle is fixed? And can models with many households and many firms be solved and estimated? The research tier of this series takes them up.
